text: Every Deployment and rolling update you've built so far in this course has relied on one quiet assumption: a Pod's own filesystem is disposable. When a Pod gets rescheduled, Kubernetes starts a brand-new container from the image with an empty writable layer. Perfect for a stateless web server. Wrong for a database that needs its data to survive past the life of one Pod. That's the problem PersistentVolumes and PersistentVolumeClaims solve.

A PersistentVolume, or PV, is a cluster-scoped object representing a real piece of storage — an Azure Disk, an AWS EBS volume, an NFS share — created independently of any one workload. This one declares a 10Gi Azure Disk is available, with a reclaim policy of Retain so the disk survives even if the claim using it is later deleted. No Pod or Deployment is mentioned anywhere in it.

A PersistentVolumeClaim is the separate, namespaced request that actually gets matched to a PV — a size and an access mode, not a specific disk by name. Kubernetes watches for both and binds a compatible pair exclusively together. Run kubectl get pvc, and a healthy claim shows STATUS Bound with a VOLUME column pointing at the PV it matched; stuck on Pending almost always means nothing available satisfied the request.

accessModes describes mount concurrency, not permissions. ReadWriteOnce means one node mounts it read-write at a time — exactly what Azure Disk and AWS EBS give you, since it's block storage attached to a single VM. ReadOnlyMany lets many nodes mount read-only. ReadWriteMany lets many nodes read-write simultaneously, but needs storage built for it, like Azure Files or NFS, never a managed disk directly.

A Pod never references a PersistentVolume directly — only the claim, by name, inside its volumes block, mounted at a path like /data. That one layer of indirection is the whole design: the same Deployment YAML can run unmodified against a completely different backing disk in a different cluster, because the application only ever asks for '10Gi, ReadWriteOnce,' never a specific disk.

Keep that Pod-to-PVC-to-PV chain straight, because next lesson removes the one manual step still sitting in it: instead of a human hand-creating a PersistentVolume ahead of time, a StorageClass lets the cloud provision the disk automatically the moment a claim asks for it.
